name: Tavas and Karafs
description: Karafs is some kind of vegetable in shape of an 1 × h rectangle. Tavaspolis people love Karafs and they use Karafs in almost any kind of food. Tavas, himself, is crazy about Karafs. Each Karafs has a positive integer height. Tavas has an infinite 1-based sequence of Karafses. The height of the i -th Karafs is s i = A + ( i - 1) × B . For a given m , let's define an m -bite operation as decreasing the height of at most m distinct not eaten Karafses by 1. Karafs is considered as eaten when its height becomes zero. Now SaDDas asks you n queries. In each query he gives you numbers l , t and m and you should find the largest number r such that l ≤ r and sequence s l , s l + 1 , ..., s r can be eaten by performing m -bite no more than t times or print -1 if there is no such number r .
input_specification: The first line of input contains three integers A , B and n ( 1 ≤ A , B ≤ 10 6 , 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ). Next n lines contain information about queries. i -th line contains integers l , t , m ( 1 ≤ l , t , m ≤ 10 6 ) for i -th query.
output_specification: For each query, print its answer in a single line.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 535C — Tavas and Karafs [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
